chunks: "A system on chip puts most of what used to be a whole computer board onto a single piece of silicon.
Instead of a separate CPU, memory controller, graphics chip, peripheral chips and so on, you integrate them as blocks on one die and connect them with an on-chip interconnect.

A typical SoC has one or more CPU cores, caches, a memory controller for external DRAM, often a GPU and other accelerators, a bunch of peripherals like UART, SPI, I2C, USB and PCIe, plus clocking, power management and security blocks.
The blocks sit in a shared address map, so software talks to a peripheral just by reading and writing registers at an address.
The reasons to do it are size, power, performance and cost at volume.
On-chip wires are shorter and cheaper to drive than board traces, so you save energy and latency, and you replace many packages with one.
Microcontrollers are really small SoCs too: a core, flash, SRAM and peripherals. A phone application processor is a big one.
It isn't free: a SoC takes a lot of design effort and a big upfront cost, and you still need things around it like DRAM, power regulators, a crystal and connectors."
